title: A private chef in Dubai, shaped around real life
intro: The pleasure of having a chef at home is not reserved for a special occasion. It can be the reassurance of knowing dinner is planned, the convenience of meals ready for a busy afternoon or the freedom to invite friends without spending the evening in the kitchen. myCHEF starts with the way you live and builds the cooking around it. The sections below help you decide which arrangement would make the biggest difference, what to include in your brief and how to prepare for a service that becomes more personal with useful feedback.

sections.title: What would you like your chef to take care of?
paragraphs: Begin with the outcome you want most. If dinner is the daily pressure point, focus the brief on evening meals. If you enjoy cooking but struggle with preparation, a weekly session may be enough. If your home needs several meals and regular kitchen support, discuss a fuller schedule.

You do not need to know the exact plan before enquiring. Tell us who is eating, when you need food and what you would like to stop managing yourself. We can then discuss a suitable chef, the visit pattern and a written scope that makes the responsibilities clear.

sections.title: Start with the meals that make your week easier
paragraphs: Think about the moments when cooking puts the most pressure on your day. It might be breakfast before school, lunch between meetings or dinner after a late journey home. Those moments tell us more about a useful chef arrangement than a long list of impressive dishes. Start with the meals you want covered and the times you want to eat, then build the schedule around them.

A household of four does not necessarily need four identical plates. One person may prefer a lighter lunch, another a larger portion after exercise, and children may want familiar flavours. Describe those differences early. The chef can then plan shared ingredients with thoughtful variations, keeping preparation realistic for the booked hours.

Consider how the plan works when you are out, too. A meal that can be finished easily later may be more useful than one that needs immediate service. This is where a personal cooking arrangement starts to feel like a practical part of home life.

sections.title: Choose the right balance of cooking days
paragraphs: More visits are useful only if they solve a real need. A focused weekly session can take care of selected meals for later, while several shorter visits may suit a household that prefers food cooked close to mealtimes. A fuller schedule makes sense when you need different meals throughout the day, more menu variety or regular kitchen support.

Write down a typical week before comparing plans. Include office days, school activities, meals out and the evenings when everyone eats together. This often reveals that two well-chosen cooking days work better than a schedule spread evenly across the week. It also helps prevent paying for preparation you rarely use.

For a changing routine, begin with a clear initial arrangement and review the portions and frequency after you have experienced it. Availability and any adjustment to the booked schedule need to be confirmed. Explore the different household options before deciding how much time you want a chef in your kitchen.

sections.title: Turn your preferences into a useful food profile
paragraphs: The most helpful food brief is specific. Tell us whether you enjoy grilled fish, dislike mushrooms, prefer mild food or want a familiar dish prepared in a particular style. Examples make it easier to translate broad preferences such as healthy, Mediterranean or family friendly into meals you genuinely want to eat.

Separate preferences from allergies and other essential restrictions. These have different implications for ingredients, substitutions and the kitchen setup. Record who each requirement applies to, rather than assuming the whole household eats the same way. If you already follow a professionally prescribed eating plan, share the relevant instructions for the proposed menu to be assessed.

Your food profile should remain useful as life changes. Add a favourite dish after a successful meal, flag portions that were too generous and tell us when guests will join. Small, clear updates give the chef a better starting point for the next menu and reduce the need to explain your preferences again.

sections.title: Agree how ingredients reach your kitchen
paragraphs: There are two practical starting points for groceries: have the agreed ingredients ready before the visit, or discuss shopping as part of the service. Either way, the menu needs a clear list. Quantities, preferred brands and acceptable alternatives help avoid delays when an ingredient is unavailable or a household staple has run out.

Keep the service fee and grocery spending easy to understand. Your written proposal should explain who shops, whether shopping time is included in the booked hours and how ingredient costs are handled. If you want a premium cut, specialist imported item or a particular organic product, include that in the brief so it can be priced and sourced appropriately.

It also helps to identify what is already in the kitchen. A quick check of oils, seasonings, rice and other staples can reduce duplicate purchases. For ongoing cooking, agree how the chef should flag low stock and ask before making substitutions that materially change the meal or its cost.

sections.title: Keep the menu interesting without making it complicated
paragraphs: A good menu has both familiarity and variety. Repeating a handful of favourite ingredients can make shopping more efficient, but repeating the same dish every visit can quickly feel limiting. Discuss a balance of reliable favourites and occasional new ideas, using different cooking methods, vegetables and accompaniments to keep meals appealing.

For example, a household that enjoys chicken might alternate a lemon and herb roast, gently spiced skewers and a lighter dish with grains and vegetables. The point is not to prescribe a fixed menu. It is to show how one preference can lead to several distinct meals that suit the available equipment and preparation time.

Ask for menus you can review easily. Clear dish descriptions are more useful than elaborate names that hide unfamiliar ingredients. If a meal is intended for reheating, check that the proposed texture and presentation will still work later. The best weekly menu is one you understand, enjoy and can use comfortably.

sections.title: Judge the service by the difference it makes at home
paragraphs: The value of a private chef is not measured only by the number of dishes prepared. Consider whether the meals are being enjoyed, whether the timing works and whether the arrangement reduces the decisions you need to make each day. A reliable favourite served when you need it can be more useful than an ambitious menu that does not fit your routine.

Review the service against the priorities in your original brief. Are the portions right? Is shopping clear? Do you understand what is ready for later? Are the booked hours being used for the tasks you care about most? These questions help you identify a practical adjustment before deciding that the whole arrangement needs to change.

For an occasion, think about your experience as host as well as the food. Clear coordination, suitable staffing and a manageable service format can give you more time with guests. The best proposal is the one that connects its price and scope to the experience you actually want.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
